name: SpookyHash V2 (Bob Jenkins' official repo)
workload: SMHasher bulk hashing throughput (large buffer, MiB/s) and per-call latency (cycles/hash on a fixed small key, cycles/map in a hash table) for SpookyV2_32/64/128 vs xxHash32/xxHash64/xxh3/xxh128 and CityHash on a single machine
claimed_speedup: SpookyV2_64 13401 MiB/s bulk vs xxHash64 11177 MiB/s bulk (~1.2x faster bulk throughput, derived from page data); but xxHash64 is faster per small-key call (49.67 cycles/hash, 230.24 cycles/map) than SpookyV2_64 (56.18 cycles/hash, 246.33 cycles/map), so SpookyV2 loses on small keys (derived from page data); xxh3 (20854 MiB/s) and City64 (14390 MiB/s) both beat SpookyV2_64 on every column (derived from page data). The bobjen/spookyhash README's own table (C++ vs its new Rust port, DoTimingSmall, no baseline hash) shows C++ reaching 19.54 GB/s at 16KB keys and 18.68 GB/s at 8KB, g++ -O3, one machine.
tradeoffs: No SIMD, plain 64-bit arithmetic with xor/barrel-shift for high ILP; 128-bit output (32/64-bit truncations available) vs xxHash64's 64-bit; repo adds a Rust port (Claude-generated) that reproduces identical hashes but runs ~7-13% slower than the C++ reference in the repo's own DoTimingSmall table.
caveats: rurban/smhasher's README states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) for its main table but not compiler or flags, so this is capped at tier B, not A, per the hard rule. SpookyV2 only wins vs xxHash64 on large-buffer bulk throughput; for small keys (cycles/hash, cycles/map) it is slower than xxHash64, and it loses to xxh3/CityHash in every column. The bobjen/spookyhash repo itself (created Mar 2026, 3 stars) is a very recent restatement of Bob Jenkins' 2012 algorithm plus a new Rust port; the SMHasher measurements are of the reference SpookyV2 C algorithm (labelled SpookyV2_32/64/128), not built from this specific repo. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication: no patent grant.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/bobjen/spookyhash (README) and https://github.com/rurban/smhasher (README results table)

name: LeMac (pauldreik C++20 port)
workload: Single-core bulk MAC/digest throughput: LeMac oneshot() hashing 256 KB/1 MB buffers vs `openssl speed -evp SHA1`, same AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D machine (Debian 13 Trixie)
claimed_speedup: ~74-77 GiB/s LeMac oneshot (median of 5 runs, 256 KB/1 MB) vs ~2.8 GiB/s OpenSSL SHA1, i.e. ~26-27x (derived from page data). Same README also reports: xxh3/xxh128 reach ~89 GiB/s via `xxhsum -b`, about 16% FASTER than LeMac (LeMac does not beat xxh3); clhash reaches 0.11 cycles/byte vs LeMac's 0.067 cycles/byte, i.e. LeMac ~39% faster than clhash; AES-128-ECB via `openssl speed -evp AES-128-ECB` reaches ~16.4 GiB/s, well below LeMac's throughput.
compiler_and_flags: cmake -B build-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (compiler not named for the Zen4/Linux run; 'compiler: clang' is stated only for the separate Apple M3/M4 runs)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, Debian 13 Trixie (primary bulk numbers, 77 GiB/s / 0.067 cycles/byte); also Apple M4 MacBook Air (48 GiB/s), Apple M3 MacBook Air, and Raspberry Pi 5 / Ubuntu 24.04 (11 GiB/s, thermally throttled per README)
tradeoffs: Requires AES-NI (amd64) or ARMv8 crypto extensions (arm64); no portable/software fallback yet (planned); ships a lemacsum CLI (sha256sum/xxhsum-style) plus a library API with reusable hasher objects to amortize ~5 KB init / ~2 KB finalize overhead; requires C++20.
caveats: README does not benchmark against either baseline named for this catalog entry (AES-GCM GHASH/GMAC or AEGIS-128L MAC); its actual comparisons are to SHA1, raw AES-128-ECB, xxh3/xxh128, and clhash, so baseline_in_list=false and this is recorded at reduced confidence. LeMac is a MAC construction, not a plain hash, so beating SHA1 (a bare digest, not itself a MAC) is not a like-for-like comparison; treat as directional evidence of AES-NI-class speed only. Compiler is not named for the primary Zen4 benchmark run (only the CMake Release build type is given), which caps this below tier B/A. Could not confirm from the README, header comments, or commit history whether this port implements the corrigendum-fixed LeMac (ToSC 2025(1)) or the original buggy LeMac-0 that corrigendum fixed; include/lemac.h states only that it is 'based on the 2024 public domain implementation (CC0-1.0) by Augustin Bariant and Gaetan Leurent' with no version/corrigendum reference.
